claim: Prominin 1 (Prom1) is a five-transmembrane pass integral membrane protein that associates with curved regions of the plasma membrane.
source: Prominin 1 (Prom1) is a five-transmembrane pass integral membrane protein that associates with curved regions of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about Prom1's structure and localization, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Prom1 interacts with membrane cholesterol and actively remodels the plasma membrane.
source: Prom1 interacts with membrane cholesterol and actively remodels the plasma membrane.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about Prom1 function.

claim: Prom1 loss-of-function mutations cause failure of outer segment homeostasis, leading to cone-rod retinal dystrophy (CRRD).
source: Membrane-bending activity is particularly evident in photoreceptors, where Prom1 loss-of-function mutations cause failure of outer segment homeostasis, leading to cone-rod retinal dystrophy (CRRD).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about Prom1 mutations and disease.

claim: The Tweety Homology (Ttyh) protein family has been proposed to be homologous to Prominin.
source: The Tweety Homology (Ttyh) protein family has been proposed to be homologous to Prominin, but it is not known whether Ttyh proteins have an analogous membrane-bending function.
evidence: This statement references prior work proposing homology between Ttyh and Prominin.

claim: It is not known whether Ttyh proteins have an analogous membrane-bending function to Prominin.
source: The Tweety Homology (Ttyh) protein family has been proposed to be homologous to Prominin, but it is not known whether Ttyh proteins have an analogous membrane-bending function.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Prom1 and Ttyh1 both induce formation of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in cultured mammalian cells.
source: We find that Prom1 and Ttyh1 both induce formation of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in cultured mammalian cells and that the EVs produced are physically similar.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EVs produced by Prom1 and Ttyh1 are physically similar.
source: We find that Prom1 and Ttyh1 both induce formation of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in cultured mammalian cells and that the EVs produced are physically similar.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing EV characteristics.

claim: Ttyh1 is more abundant in EV membranes than Prom1.
source: Ttyh1 is more abundant in EV membranes than Prom1 and produces EVs with membranes that are more tubulated than Prom1 EVs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ttyh1 produces EVs with membranes that are more tubulated than Prom1 EVs.
source: Ttyh1 is more abundant in EV membranes than Prom1 and produces EVs with membranes that are more tubulated than Prom1 EVs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data showing EV morphology.

claim: Prom1 interacts more stably with membrane cholesterol than Ttyh1.
source: We further show that Prom1 interacts more stably with membrane cholesterol than Ttyh1 and that this may contribute to membrane-bending inhibition in Prom1 EVs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cholesterol co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: Stable cholesterol binding by Prom1 may contribute to membrane-bending inhibition in Prom1 EVs.
source: We further show that Prom1 interacts more stably with membrane cholesterol than Ttyh1 and that this may contribute to membrane-bending inhibition in Prom1 EVs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data involving speculation about mechanism.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in Prom1 associated with CRRD (W795R) induces particularly stable cholesterol binding.
source: Intriguingly, a loss-of-function mutation in Prom1 associated with CRRD induces particularly stable cholesterol binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cholesterol binding assays with the W795R mutant.

claim: Prom1 was first characterized as the target of AC133-1, a monoclonal antibody raised against pluripotent human epithelial stem cells.
source: Prom1 was first characterized as the target of AC133-1, a monoclonal antibody raised against pluripotent human epithelial stem cells (Yin et al., 1997; Miraglia et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prom1 has been identified in the apical membranes of most epithelial and neuroepithelial cell types.
source: Since then, Prom1 has been identified in the apical membranes of most epithelial and neuroepithelial cell types, but is only natively recognized by AC133-1 in stem cells and photoreceptors (Corbeil et al., 1998; Kemper et al., 2010b; Mak et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prom1 is only natively recognized by AC133-1 in stem cells and photoreceptors.
source: Since then, Prom1 has been identified in the apical membranes of most epithelial and neuroepithelial cell types, but is only natively recognized by AC133-1 in stem cells and photoreceptors (Corbeil et al., 1998; Kemper et al., 2010b; Mak et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In photoreceptors, Prom1 associates with a retinal cadherin (Protocadherin-21, Pcdh21) to promote normal outer segment membrane homeostasis.
source: In photoreceptors, Prom1 associates with a retinal cadherin (Protocadherin-21, Pcdh21) to promote normal outer segment membrane homeostasis (Yang et al., 2008; Burgoyne et al., 2015; Rattner et al., 2001), and several Prom1 mutations are linked to hereditary cone-rod retinal dystrophy (CRRD) (Yang et al., 2008; Zacchigna et al., 2009; Eidinger et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2019; Maw et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several Prom1 mutations are linked to hereditary cone-rod retinal dystrophy (CRRD).
source: In photoreceptors, Prom1 associates with a retinal cadherin (Protocadherin-21, Pcdh21) to promote normal outer segment membrane homeostasis (Yang et al., 2008; Burgoyne et al., 2015; Rattner et al., 2001), and several Prom1 mutations are linked to hereditary cone-rod retinal dystrophy (CRRD) (Yang et al., 2008; Zacchigna et al., 2009; Eidinger et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2019; Maw et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most animal genomes encode at least one paralogous prominin gene (Prominin 2) that is expressed in non-retinal cell types and localizes to positively curved membrane regions.
source: Most animal genomes also encode at least one paralogous prominin gene (Prominin 2) that is expressed in non-retinal cell types and localizes to positively curved membrane regions (Fargeas, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When overexpressed, Prom1 dramatically reorganizes the plasma membrane of cultured mammalian cells into long protrusions.
source: When overexpressed, Prom1 dramatically reorganizes the plasma membrane of cultured mammalian cells into long protrusions (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Small-molecule inhibitors of actin and tubulin do not impair the tubulation phenotype of Prom1.
source: Small-molecule inhibitors of actin and tubulin do not impair the tubulation phenotype, indicating that cytoskeletal interactions are not strictly required for membrane bending (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cytoskeletal interactions are not strictly required for membrane bending by Prom1.
source: Small-molecule inhibitors of actin and tubulin do not impair the tubulation phenotype, indicating that cytoskeletal interactions are not strictly required for membrane bending (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is an inference from experimental data cited from prior work.

claim: Cells treated with cholesterol biosynthesis inhibitors or depletion agents do not exhibit membrane tubulation by Prom1.
source: However, cells treated with cholesterol biosynthesis inhibitors or depletion agents do not exhibit membrane tubulation, suggesting that cholesterol plays a pivotal role in the regulation of Prom1 function (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cholesterol plays a pivotal role in the regulation of Prom1 function.
source: However, cells treated with cholesterol biosynthesis inhibitors or depletion agents do not exhibit membrane tubulation, suggesting that cholesterol plays a pivotal role in the regulation of Prom1 function (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is an inference from experimental data cited from prior work.

claim: Prom1 induces release of small extracellular vesicles (EVs, <250 nm in diameter) that bleb from the apical plasma membrane of differentiating epithelial stem cells at organized membrane protrusions such as microvilli and cilia.
source: Prom1 also induces release of small extracellular vesicles (EVs, <250 nm in diameter) that bleb from the apical plasma membrane of differentiating epithelial stem cells at organized membrane protrusions such as microvilli and cilia (Marzesco et al., 2005; Wood and Rosenbaum, 2015; Dubreuil et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Small Prom1 EVs can be detected in saliva, urine, semen, neural tube fluid, and lacrimal fluid of healthy adults.
source: Small Prom1 EVs can be detected in saliva, urine, semen, neural tube fluid, and lacrimal fluid of healthy adults (Marzesco et al., 2005; Hurbain et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ttyh proteins share prominins' five-transmembrane topology but have a more minimal extracellular domain.
source: Ttyh proteins share prominins' five-transmembrane topology but have a more minimal extracellular domain (Campbell et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most animals have three paralogous Ttyh proteins (Ttyh1, Ttyh2, and Ttyh3).
source: Most animals have three paralogous Ttyh proteins (Ttyh1, Ttyh2, and Ttyh3) (Matthews et al., 2007) that all are predominantly expressed in neural tissues (Halleran et al., 2015; Bae et al., 2019; Han et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Sukalskaia et al., 2021; Melvin et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ttyh proteins are predominantly expressed in neural tissues.
source: Most animals have three paralogous Ttyh proteins (Ttyh1, Ttyh2, and Ttyh3) (Matthews et al., 2007) that all are predominantly expressed in neural tissues (Halleran et al., 2015; Bae et al., 2019; Han et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Sukalskaia et al., 2021; Melvin et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of Ttyh1 at the plasma membrane in cultured cells induces plasma membrane tubulation that is strikingly similar to that observed with Prom1.
source: Notably, overexpression of Ttyh1 at the plasma membrane in cultured cells induces plasma membrane tubulation that is strikingly similar to that observed with Prom1 (Matthews et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2017; Stefaniuk et al., 2010; Wiernasz et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C-terminally Strep-tagged Prom1 was detected in immunoblots of the conditioned media (CM) from transfected cells, but not in cells treated with a no-plasmid mock transfection.
source: C-terminally Strep-tagged Prom1 was detected in immunoblots of the conditioned media (CM) from transfected cells, but not in cells treated with a no-plasmid mock transfection (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ~120 kDa Strep-reactive band observed in immunoblots is Prom1-Strep, as confirmed by AC133-1 antibody staining.
source: To validate that the ~120 kDa Strep-reactive band we observe is indeed Prom1-Strep, we immunoblotted with the Prom1-specific antibody AC133-1 (Kemper et al., 2010a) and observed robust staining (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A Strep-reactive band consistent with mature Prom1 was detectable in the CM from stable polyclonal Expi293 cells expressing Prom1-Strep over several rounds of cell passaging.
source: To confirm that EV production is not an artifact of transfection, we introduced Prom1-Strep into Expi293 cells by lentiviral transduction to generate a stable polyclonal overexpression cell line. A Strep-reactive band consistent with mature Prom1 was detectable in the CM from these cells over several rounds of cell passaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Prom1 was a constituent of purified EV samples alongside several other proteins.
source: We assessed the protein composition of Prom1 EVs using sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) and silver nitrate staining. Prom1 was a constituent of our samples alongside several other proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purified Prom1 EVs have an average diameter of 164 ± 14 nm as measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS).
source: Using dynamic light scattering (DLS), we measured the solution sizes of the purified Prom1 EVs. The sample was monodisperse with an average diameter of 164 ± 14 nm, considerably larger than previously reported 50–80 nm EVs measured by negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (NS-TEM) in samples purified from biological fluids (Marzesco et al., 2005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from DLS measurements.

claim: Purified Prom1 EVs are considerably larger than previously reported 50–80 nm EVs measured by negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (NS-TEM) in samples purified from biological fluids.
source: Using dynamic light scattering (DLS), we measured the solution sizes of the purified Prom1 EVs. The sample was monodisperse with an average diameter of 164 ± 14 nm, considerably larger than previously reported 50–80 nm EVs measured by negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (NS-TEM) in samples purified from biological fluids (Marzesco et al., 2005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement compares current data with prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Upon treatment with PNGase F, the ~120 kDa Prom1 gel band shifted down to its predicted molecular weight of 102 kDa.
source: Upon treatment with PNGase F, an enzyme that cleaves N-glycan groups from proteins, the ~120 kDa Prom1 gel band shifted down to its predicted molecular weight of 102 kDa (Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Purified Prom1 particles are spherical EVs with bilayer membranes as observed by cryo-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM).
source: To verify that the purified particles are truly EVs (secreted particles with intact bilayer membranes), we vitrified purified samples and imaged them using cryo-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) (Figure 1E). We observed spherical EVs with bilayer membranes (Figure 1E, inset).
evidence: This statement is supported by cryo-TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The diameters of Prom1 EVs measured from cryo-TEM images were bimodal with an average diameter of 117 ± 58 nm.
source: The diameters of EVs measured from cryo-TEM images were bimodal with an average diameter of 117 ± 58 nm, somewhat lower than our measurements from DLS (Figure 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-TEM images shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Prom1 EVs observed by NS-TEM have a distribution of largely circular EVs ranging in size from ~50 to ~250 nm in diameter, but more skewed toward smaller diameters than observed in the cryo-TEM data.
source: We next used NS-TEM to directly compare our reconstituted Prom1 EVs with previously characterized endogenous Prom1 EVs (Marzesco et al., 2005; Figure 1F). We observed a distribution of largely circular EVs ranging in size from ~50 to ~250 nm in diameter, but more skewed toward smaller diameters than observed in the cryo-TEM data (Figure 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by NS-TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1F and quantification in Figure 1G.

claim: Prom1 EVs had rough edges and internal depressions in NS-TEM, a characteristic feature of EV fixation and dehydration.
source: In addition, EVs had rough edges and internal depressions in NS-TEM, a characteristic feature of EV fixation and dehydration (Marzesco et al., 2005; Figure 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by NS-TEM imaging data and comparison with prior work.

claim: Sample fixation/dehydration or vitrification may induce deformation and potentially fission of the reconstituted EVs.
source: Because solution DLS measurements (164 ± 14 nm) suggest slightly larger EV diameters than our NS-TEM (123 ± 73 nm) or cryo-TEM (117 ± 58 nm) measurements, we speculate that sample fixation/dehydration or vitrification may induce deformation and potentially fission of the reconstituted EVs.
evidence: This statement is speculation based on comparison of different measurement methods.

claim: Reconstituted Prom1 EVs have similar morphology to endogenous EVs but may be slightly larger in size.
source: We conclude that reconstituted Prom1 EVs have similar morphology to endogenous EVs but may be slightly larger in size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of experimental data with prior work.

claim: Prom1 stably binds the retinal cadherin Pcdh21 in photoreceptors.
source: We next asked whether Prom1 in purified EVs retains known functional behavior of Prom1 from endogenous membranes. Prom1 stably binds the retinal cadherin Pcdh21 in photoreceptors (Yang et al., 2008; Burgoyne et al., 2015; Rattner et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pcdh21 was only observed in CCM samples when co-expressed with Prom1, indicating that Prom1 is necessary to traffic Pcdh21 into this class of EVs.
source: To determine if Prom1 can co-traffic with Pcdh21 in our EV samples, we co-transfected Expi293 cells with Strep-tagged Prom1 and Flag-tagged Pcdh21 and looked for the presence of each component in cells, CM, and clarified conditioned media (CCM). Pcdh21 was only observed in CCM samples when co-expressed with Prom1, indicating that Prom1 is necessary to traffic Pcdh21 into this class of EVs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Pcdh21 physically interacts with Prom1 in purified EVs.
source: To establish a direct interaction between Prom1 and Pcdh21, we co-expressed Prom1-Strep with mNeonGreen-tagged Pcdh21 and immunopurified Prom1 from EVs solubilized with 1% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM). Pcdh21-associated mNeonGreen reproducibly co-purified with detergent-solubilized Prom1 compared to a control condition lacking Prom1, indicating that the two proteins physically interact in purified EVs (Figure 1I).
evidence: This statement is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Human Prom1 contained four CRAC and two CARC motifs, of which none were completely conserved among metazoans and only one (CRAC-3) was modestly evolutionarily conserved.
source: Human Prom1 contained four CRAC and two CARC motifs, of which none were completely conserved among metazoans and only one (CRAC-3) was modestly evolutionarily conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trp-795 was nearly perfectly conserved across metazoa and eukaryotic outgroups, making it by far the most conserved residue (excluding Cys residues positioned to form disulfides in AlphaFold2 models) across the curated prominin sequences.
source: Strikingly, Trp-795 was nearly perfectly conserved across metazoa and eukaryotic outgroups, making it by far the most conserved residue (excluding Cys residues positioned to form disulfides in AlphaFold2 models) across the curated prominin sequences (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A missense mutation at Trp-795 (W795R) is implicated in hereditary CRRD cases.
source: The conserved Trp-795 residue was of particular interest as a missense mutation at this site (W795R) is implicated in hereditary CRRD cases (Boulanger-Scemama et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The W795R mutation to the Prom1 TM domain significantly disrupted the proportion of Prom1 secreted in EVs.
source: We found that the W795R mutation to the Prom1 TM domain significantly disrupted the proportion of Prom1 secreted in EVs (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 for raw blot images).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The W795R mutation effect on EV secretion arose from both decreased expression of Prom1 and increased retention of protein in cells.
source: This effect arose from both decreased expression of Prom1 and increased retention of protein in cells, though neither of these measurements alone met our stringent significance criteria.
evidence: This statement is an interpretation of experimental data.

claim: Each of the Prom1 mutants produced EVs that are 150–200 nm in diameter and monodisperse by DLS analysis.
source: To better characterize the morphology of the Prom1 variants, we expressed and purified a subset of mutant Prom1 EVs at larger scale. Each of the mutants produced EVs that are 150–200 nm in diameter and monodisperse by DLS analysis, with no mutant EV sizes deviating significantly from that of WT Prom1 EVs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by DLS measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Transmembrane domain mutations in Prom1 primarily alter the quantity of EVs produced rather than EV size.
source: Thus, transmembrane domain mutations in Prom1 primarily alter the quantity of EVs produced rather than EV size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on mutant EVs.

claim: Prom1-SG signal colocalized with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-stained plasma membrane.
source: Prom1-SG signal colocalized with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-stained plasma membrane, but Prom1[W795R]-SG was not present at the plasma membrane and instead concentrated on WGA-positive intracellular features (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Prom1[W795R]-SG was not present at the plasma membrane and instead concentrated on WGA-positive intracellular features.
source: Prom1-SG signal colocalized with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-stained plasma membrane, but Prom1[W795R]-SG was not present at the plasma membrane and instead concentrated on WGA-positive intracellular features (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mStayGold-tagged W795R Prom1 is trafficked to the plasma membrane less efficiently than the mStayGold-tagged wild-type protein.
source: We infer that mStayGold-tagged W795R Prom1 is trafficked to the plasma membrane less efficiently than the mStayGold-tagged wild-type protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Prominin and Ttyh both traffic to the plasma membrane and associate with protrusive membrane structures.
source: Prominin and Ttyh both traffic to the plasma membrane and associate with protrusive membrane structures (Hori et al., 2019; Röper et al., 2000; Matthews et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2017; Stefaniuk et al., 2010; Wiernasz et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Evolutionary analysis of metazoan Ttyh proteins does not indicate conserved CRAC or CARC sites, nor does it suggest any conserved transmembrane residue analogous to Trp-795 in metazoan prominins.
source: Evolutionary analysis of metazoan Ttyh proteins does not indicate conserved CRAC or CARC sites, nor does it suggest any conserved transmembrane residue analogous to Trp-795 in metazoan prominins (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is supported by evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ttyh1-Strep was detected in CM, CCM, and SEC-purified EV fractions.
source: We expressed C-terminally Strep-tagged Ttyh1 in Expi293 cells and purified EVs using the same procedure as for Prom1 EVs (Figure 1A). We detected Ttyh1-Strep in CM, CCM, and SEC-purified EV fractions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Purified Ttyh1 EVs are monodisperse with an average diameter of 180 ± 10 nm, similar to the average diameter of WT Prom1 EVs (164 ± 14 nm).
source: DLS indicated that purified Ttyh1 EVs are monodisperse with an average diameter of 180 ± 10 nm, similar to the average diameter of WT Prom1 EVs (164 ± 14 nm) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by DLS measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ttyh EVs adopted striking long and bent tubular structures with much higher frequency than Prom1 EVs (6.4% of Ttyh1 EVs vs 0.3% of Prom1 EVs).
source: We next characterized the morphology of purified Ttyh1 EVs using NS-TEM. We found that Ttyh EVs adopted striking long and bent tubular structures with much higher frequency than Prom1 EVs (6.4% of Ttyh1 EVs vs 0.3% of Prom1 EVs, n = 1357 and n = 322, respectively) (Figure 3D, G).
evidence: This statement is supported by NS-TEM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3D and 3G.

claim: Ttyh1 EVs visualized by NS-TEM were on average smaller than Prom1 EVs.
source: Ttyh1 EVs visualized by NS-TEM were on average smaller than Prom1 EVs (Figure 3F, G), and were similarly smaller than expected from solution DLS measurement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantification of NS-TEM images shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The smallest Ttyh1 EVs were similar in diameter to the short-axis caliper diameter of the tubular EVs (42 ± 6 nm).
source: Furthermore, we observed that the smallest Ttyh1 EVs were similar in diameter to the short-axis caliper diameter of the tubular EVs (42 ± 6 nm) and we observed cases where tubular EVs appeared to be in the process of dividing into smaller EVs (Figure 3D white arrowheads, Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by measurements from NS-TEM images.

claim: Tubular Ttyh1 EVs appeared to be in the process of dividing into smaller EVs.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the smallest Ttyh1 EVs were similar in diameter to the short-axis caliper diameter of the tubular EVs (42 ± 6 nm) and we observed cases where tubular EVs appeared to be in the process of dividing into smaller EVs (Figure 3D white arrowheads, Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is an observation from NS-TEM images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ttyh1 supports comparatively greater membrane curvature than Prom1 in these EVs.
source: Although the NS-TEM conditions deviate from a solvated physiological state, they do suggest that Ttyh1 supports comparatively greater membrane curvature than Prom1 in these EVs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from NS-TEM observations.

claim: Ttyh1 EVs have a bimodal size distribution with local maxima around 60 and 140 nm.
source: We further analyzed Ttyh1 EVs by cryo-TEM to verify that the purified sample indeed contained EVs with intact bilayer membranes (Figure 3E). Like Prom1 EVs, Ttyh1 EVs have a bimodal size distribution with local maxima around 60 and 140 nm (Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by cryo-TEM data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: A population of Ttyh1 EVs exhibiting the tubular phenotype seen in NS-TEM substantially exceeded that seen with Prom1 EVs (8.8% of Ttyh1 EVs vs 0.8% of Prom1 EVs) in cryo-TEM.
source: We also observed a population of EVs exhibiting the tubular phenotype seen in NS-TEM that again substantially exceeded that seen with Prom1 EVs (8.8% of Ttyh1 EVs vs 0.8% of Prom1 EVs, n = 2224 and n = 176, respectively) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantification of cryo-TEM images shown in Figure 3G.

claim: From identical amounts of transfected cell media, purified EVs contained 8.8 ± 1.0 fold more Ttyh1 protein than Prom1.
source: From identical amounts of transfected cell media, purified EVs contained 8.8 ± 1.0 fold more Ttyh1 protein than Prom1 (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative immunoblot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Both Prom1 and Ttyh1 EV membrane surface areas were significantly more abundant than the background level of EVs produced in a mock-transfected control culture.
source: Both Prom1 and Ttyh1 EV membrane surface areas were significantly more abundant than the background level of EVs produced in a mock-transfected control culture, but Ttyh1 produced 5.6 ± 0.8 fold more total EV membrane than Prom1 (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantification of membrane area from NS-TEM images shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ttyh1 produced 5.6 ± 0.8 fold more total EV membrane than Prom1.
source: Both Prom1 and Ttyh1 EV membrane surface areas were significantly more abundant than the background level of EVs produced in a mock-transfected control culture, but Ttyh1 produced 5.6 ± 0.8 fold more total EV membrane than Prom1 (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantification of membrane area from NS-TEM images shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ttyh1 is present at ~fivefold higher concentration in EV membranes than Prom1.
source: From these measurements, we estimate that Ttyh1 is present at ~fivefold higher concentration in EV membranes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an estimate derived from protein and membrane quantification data.

claim: Molecular-crowding effects may be a factor contributing to the increased membrane bending observed in Ttyh1 EVs.
source: Thus, molecular-crowding effects may be a factor contributing to the increased membrane bending we observe in Ttyh1 EVs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the protein-to-membrane ratio measurements.

claim: A single population of Prom1 EVs (centered on fraction 7) was observed in equilibrium sucrose gradient sedimentation.
source: To further characterize purified Prom1 and Ttyh1 EVs, we subjected purified EVs to equilibrium sucrose gradient sedimentation to resolve populations by density. We observed a single population of Prom1 EVs (centered on fraction 7) but resolved two distinct populations of Ttyh1 EVs with densities lower (centered on fraction 6) and higher (centered on fraction 9) than the Prom1 EVs (Figure 3J).
evidence: This statement is supported by sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Two distinct populations of Ttyh1 EVs with densities lower (centered on fraction 6) and higher (centered on fraction 9) than the Prom1 EVs were resolved by equilibrium sucrose gradient sedimentation.
source: To further characterize purified Prom1 and Ttyh1 EVs, we subjected purified EVs to equilibrium sucrose gradient sedimentation to resolve populations by density. We observed a single population of Prom1 EVs (centered on fraction 7) but resolved two distinct populations of Ttyh1 EVs with densities lower (centered on fraction 6) and higher (centered on fraction 9) than the Prom1 EVs (Figure 3J).
evidence: This statement is supported by sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: When Prom1 and Ttyh1 were co-expressed, the resulting EVs contained more Prom1 than Ttyh1 but followed the bimodal distribution of Ttyh1 EVs.
source: When Prom1 and Ttyh1 were co-expressed, we observed that the resulting EVs contained more Prom1 than Ttyh1 but followed the bimodal distribution of Ttyh1 EVs (Figure 3K).
evidence: This statement is supported by sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Co-expressed Prom1 and Ttyh1 peak in the same sucrose gradient fractions, suggesting that Prom1 and Ttyh1 co-elute in the same EV populations.
source: Immunoblots of the sucrose gradient fractions showed that co-expressed Prom1 and Ttyh1 peak in the same sucrose gradient fractions, suggesting that Prom1 and Ttyh1 co-elute in the same EV populations (Figure 3K, L).
evidence: This statement is an inference from sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 3K and 3L.

claim: Fluorescent cholesterol robustly co-purified with Prom1 but not with Ttyh1 in chol-IP analysis.
source: We performed chol-IP analysis on Prom1 or Ttyh1 EVs labeled with BODIPY-cholesterol. Surprisingly, fluorescent cholesterol robustly co-purified with Prom1 but not with Ttyh1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is supported by chol-IP assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in cholesterol binding between Prom1 and Ttyh1 is not a result of nonspecific fluorophore–protein interactions.
source: To verify that this difference is not a result of nonspecific fluorophore–protein interactions, we replicated the observation using a different fluorescent cholesterol analog (AlexaFluor647-cholesterol) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by replication with a different fluorescent cholesterol analog shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nonspecifically associated fluorescent cholesterol in Ttyh1 samples is delipidated at 0.04–0.2% DDM, 5- to 25-fold below the assay working concentration.
source: We further verified that the cholesterol is specifically bound to Prom1 by quantifying bound cholesterol at different concentrations of solubilizing detergent (Figure 4C). Nonspecifically associated fluorescent cholesterol in Ttyh1 samples is delipidated at 0.04–0.2% DDM, 5- to 25-fold below the assay working concentration, suggesting that the assay informs on specific lipid binding that is resistant to delipidation.
evidence: This statement is supported by detergent titration data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Prom1 and Ttyh1 differ in how stably they interact with membrane cholesterol.
source: Although this method cannot inform on transient or kinetically unstable protein–lipid interactions, we infer that Prom1 and Ttyh1 differ in how stably they interact with membrane cholesterol.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chol-IP assay results.

claim: None of the Prom1 mutants substantially disrupted cholesterol binding, but the W795R mutant and the CARC-1 mutants bound cholesterol significantly more stably than WT Prom1.
source: We purified BODIPY-cholesterol-labeled EVs produced by WT and mutant forms of Prom1 and subjected equal input concentrations of Prom1 to chol-IP analysis. To our surprise, none of the mutants substantially disrupted cholesterol binding, but the W795R mutant and the CARC-1 mutants bound cholesterol significantly more stably than WT Prom1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by chol-IP assay data on mutants shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Prom1 W795R co-purified with ~60% as much mScarlet fluorescence as WT Prom1, indicating that W795R indeed multimerizes, albeit with reduced efficiency.
source: To verify that differences in cholesterol binding between wild-type and W795R Prom1 do not arise from a gross oligomerization defect, we purified EVs from cells co-transfected with Strep- and mScarlet-tagged Prom1 and measured co-purification of Prom1-mScarlet on Strep resin. Prom1 W795R co-purified with ~60% as much mScarlet fluorescence as WT Prom1, indicating that W795R indeed multimerizes, albeit with reduced efficiency (Figure 4E).
evidence: This statement is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There may be a weak inverse correlation between EV yield and stable cholesterol binding, but W795R, CARC-1, and CARC-2 are outliers that bind cholesterol exceptionally tightly.
source: Comparative analysis of EV Yield (Figure 2C) and cholesterol bound (Figure 4D) indicates that though there may be a weak inverse correlation between cholesterol binding and stable cholesterol binding, W795R, CARC-1, and CARC-2 are outliers that bind cholesterol exceptionally tightly (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparative analysis of data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: WT and W795R Prom1 EVs have similar solution sizes (164 ± 14 nm for WT and 186 ± 13 nm for W795R).
source: After purifying W795R Prom1 EVs, we observed a similar solution size for WT (164 ± 14 nm) and W795R EVs (186 ± 13 nm) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by DLS measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT and W795R Prom1 EVs are both spherical, with W795R having no vesicles that fall into the tubular morphology classification.
source: We measured the size and shape of W795R EVs by cryo-TEM and observed largely spherical vesicles with some local deformations, similar to what we observed with WT Prom1 EVs (Figure 5A). Generally, WT and W795R Prom1 EVs are both spherical, with W795R having no vesicles that fall into our tubular morphology classification (n = 1211) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by cryo-TEM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: W795R Prom1 had a larger fraction of small EVs than WT Prom1, indicating possible decreased stability or increased fissile propensity in the W795R Prom1 EVs.
source: Though both large and small diameter EV populations were observed by cryo-TEM, W795R Prom1 had a larger fraction of small EVs than WT Prom1, indicating possible decreased stability or increased fissile propensity in the W795R Prom1 EVs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by cryo-TEM data shown in Figure 5C and includes speculation about mechanism.

claim: Prom1 EVs treated with mBCD (2.5–10 mM) exhibited a decrease in cholesterol content.
source: We tested this model directly by purifying WT Prom1 or Ttyh1 EVs and treating them with methyl-beta cyclodextrin (mBCD), a compound that extracts cholesterol from membranes (Röper et al., 2000; Zidovetzki and Levitan, 2007). After re-purifying EV samples away from free mBCD and mBCD–cholesterol complexes, Prom1 EVs treated with mBCD (2.5–10 mM) exhibited a decrease in cholesterol content (Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by cholesterol quantification data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A 5.4-fold increase in the fraction of Prom1 EVs that deviated from spherical membrane topology was observed after 10 mM mBCD treatment compared to untreated EVs (3.0% vs 0.6% of EVs).
source: Treated and untreated EVs were then analyzed by NS-TEM to compare EV size and morphology (Figure 5E). We observed a 5.4-fold increase in the fraction of Prom1 EVs that deviated from spherical membrane topology after 10 mM mBCD treatment compared to untreated EVs (3.0% vs 0.6% of EVs, n = 232 and n = 356, respectively) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This statement is supported by NS-TEM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Ttyh1 EVs treated with mBCD under identical conditions only showed a 1.4-fold increase in deformed EVs (2.1% at 10 mM mBCD vs 1.5% in mock-treated EVs).
source: Importantly, identical treatment of Ttyh1 EVs was used as a nonspecific control for cholesterol depletion from EVs. Ttyh1 EVs treated with mBCD under identical conditions only showed a 1.4-fold increase in deformed EVs (2.1% at 10 mM mBCD vs 1.5% in mock-treated EVs, n = 433 and n = 535, respectively) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This statement is supported by NS-TEM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cholesterol-depleted Prom1 EVs are more prone to membrane deformation than untreated EVs.
source: Thus, cholesterol-depleted Prom1 EVs are more prone to membrane deformation than untreated EVs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mBCD treatment experiments.

claim: Ttyh1 EVs may form by a similar mechanism to Prom1 EV formation.
source: Though we have not examined whether Ttyh1 endogenously induces EV formation, we note that it is sufficient to do so in a recombinant system with similar or higher efficiency than Prom1. Given similar membrane remodeling behavior of Prom1 and Ttyh1 in cell culture (Hori et al., 2019; Stefaniuk et al., 2010), Ttyh1 EVs may form by a similar mechanism to Prom1 EV formation.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed similarities between Prom1 and Ttyh1 EV formation.

claim: Photoreceptors with impaired expression of the disc rim stabilizing protein Peripherin accumulate EVs 200–280 nm in diameter at the outer segment base.
source: Membrane bending by Prom1 is critical for maintaining outer segment membrane homeostasis in photoreceptors. Intriguingly, photoreceptors with impaired expression of the disc rim stabilizing protein Peripherin accumulate EVs 200–280 nm in diameter at the outer segment base (Salinas et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Curvature-stabilizing proteins like Peripherin may prevent the evaginating membrane from budding into EVs.
source: This may be an example of endogenous regulation of Prom1-induced membrane curvature, with curvature-stabilizing proteins like Peripherin preventing the evaginating membrane from budding into EVs.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of Peripherin in regulating Prom1 function.

claim: Membrane proteins can induce curvature through molecular crowding when enriched at sufficiently high local concentrations.
source: Several factors could contribute to this increase in membrane bending. First, Ttyh1 is present in EVs at concentrations approximately fivefold higher than Prom1 (Figure 3H, I). Membrane proteins can induce curvature through molecular crowding when enriched at sufficiently high local concentrations (Derganc and Čopič, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on membrane protein crowding.

claim: Protein trafficking through the endomembrane system is sensitive to cholesterol levels.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that protein trafficking through the endomembrane system is sensitive to cholesterol levels (Ridsdale et al., 2006; Stüven et al., 2003), and our findings may suggest an as-yet undefined role for cholesterol in Prom1 membrane trafficking as well.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The findings may suggest an as-yet undefined role for cholesterol in Prom1 membrane trafficking.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that protein trafficking through the endomembrane system is sensitive to cholesterol levels (Ridsdale et al., 2006; Stüven et al., 2003), and our findings may suggest an as-yet undefined role for cholesterol in Prom1 membrane trafficking as well.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential role for cholesterol in Prom1 trafficking based on the current findings.

claim: Prominins localize to cholesterol-rich domains of the plasma membrane and drive protrusion-shed EV formation in differentiating stem cells.
source: Prominin and Ttyh proteins are both biologically implicated in membrane bending. Prominins localize to cholesterol-rich domains of the plasma membrane and drive protrusion-shed EV formation in differentiating stem cells (Röper et al., 2000; Marzesco et al., 2005; Dubreuil et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ttyh proteins are associated with dendritic spikes in healthy neurons and with tumor microtube formation in aggressive astrocytoma.
source: Ttyh proteins are associated with dendritic spikes in healthy neurons and with tumor microtube formation in aggressive astrocytoma (Matthews et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2017; Stefaniuk et al., 2010; Wiernasz et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prom and Ttyh proteins should be considered members of a broader prominin family of membrane remodeling proteins.
source: Given their sequence homology and transmembrane topology, and their similarities in membrane localization, membrane bending, and EV formation behavior, we suggest that Prom and Ttyh proteins be considered members of a broader prominin family of membrane remodeling proteins.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the collective findings of the study.
